newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania faces anarchy as unrest, looting spread.
newsitem.headline: Albania faces anarchy as unrest, looting spread.

text.p: Albania slid towards anarchy on Thursday as arms depots in several towns including the capital Tirana were looted and people used the weapons to raid food warehouses for emergency stockpiles.

As gunfire crackled around the capital in an orgy of celebration, Tirana airport was closed after a nearby military base was looted, preventing the evacuation of some foreign embassy staff ordered out by their governments.
President Sali Berisha and all Albanian political parties called for NATO's European members to provide military assistance to Tirana to restore order in the Balkan country.

The appeal to the Western European Union said all political forces in Albania agreed outside military assistance was needed "to restore the constitutional order and to preserve the country's integrity".

A European mediation mission headed by former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky was due to fly into Tirana on Thursday to resume efforts to end the chaos. Vranitzky said he would try to reach the capital later in the day.
In the northern city of Shkoder, until now untouched by the armed rebellion sweeping the country, doctors said five people had died and 50 were wounded as two arms depots were looted.
Albanian state television listed another four towns in the north and the southeast where rebels had looted arms.
In Tirana, many shops and businesses closed and women queued for bread at bakeries.

The United States military in Germany said it had put a naval battle group on standby in the Adriatic Sea in case Washington decided to use troops to evacuate more than 2,000 Americans living in Albania.
Britain said it was planning to evacuate more than 120 British, Irish and Canadian citizens. It told them to turn up at the British embassy with passports and hand luggage.
They were expected to leave on a British naval vessel from Durres, perhaps as early as Thursday, although reporters visiting the town said the port was closed.

Up to 400 Albanians were reported to have stormed aboard a merchant ship in Durres and forced it to set sail for the southern Italian port of Brindisi, which it was approaching under an Italian navy escort.

Unlike rebels who have seized control of the south in an anti-government uprising sparked by anger over the collapse of pyramid savings schemes, looters in the north appeared to be arming themselves for self-protection.
"We are not against the president or the government, we just want to protect ourselves," one man in a village outside the capital said as he shouldered a captured Kalashnikov automatic rifle.

In Athens, the Defence Ministry said a Greek navy minesweeper was waiting off the coast near the rebel-held southern Albanian port of Sarande until local leaders organised themselves to receive its cargo of food and medicine.
Rebels in the south say Berisha allowed the pyramid schemes to flourish and did not warn people of the risks. They want him to quit before they hand in their weapons.
A new all-party government demanded by the rebels, and approved by Berisha on Wednesday, was sworn in on Thursday.

Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, a Socialist from Gjirokaster, one of the southern towns now in rebel hands, said on Wednesday evening: "After consultations with all political forces we have tried to make a government for all Albanians.
"I call on Albanians in these times to think about Albania, not political forces."
Fino said he wanted to open a dialogue with the rebels in the south.
Fresh appeals for calm were broadcast on Albanian television by the mayor of Tirana and the member of parliament for the area around the airport, a scene of recent looting.
Tirana residents woke on Thursday to find the military academy and other arms depots in the area had been looted of weapons and other equipment during the night.
Hundreds of civilians, some armed, raided a large Swiss-owned warehouse in a suburb of Tirana and made off with 650 tonnes of flour in trucks, on donkeys and on bicycles.
Members of the Shik secret police armed with rifles arrived on the scene but left soon afterwards without intervening. There was virtually no uniformed police presence in the city.
Outside the capital the situation was equally chaotic as arms depots were raided, and nearly all able-bodied men were carrying weapons of some sort, many firing them into the air.
In the town of Lac, 45 km (30 miles) north of Tirana, a Reuters correspondent saw a crowd of several hundred people force the police to release some 40 prisoners from police cells.
